title: Abdusattorov, Woodward Start With Wins In London Chess Classic
summary:
GMs Nodirbek Abdusattorov and Andy Woodward started with wins in round one of the XTX Markets London Chess Classic 2026 on Wednesday. Defending Champion Abdusattorov (with White) defeated GM Shreyas Royal in a Benoni pawn structure with reversed colors, while Woodward had the black pieces in a Sicilian duel with GM Ihor Samunenkov.

Round two is on Thursday, November 26, starting at 11 a.m. ET / 17:00 CET / 9:30 p.m. IST.

Abdusattorov and Woodward are in the lead, but there are eight rounds to go.

Standings After Round 1

All the other games ended in draws—not without missed chances!—as you can see in the results graphic below.

The London Chess Classic, first held in 2009, is back for its fourth edition since 2020. COVID-19 caused a three-year interruption, but since 2023 the UK's most prestigious invitational tournament has been an annual recurrence.

Abdusattorov won last year's edition by a remarkable two-point margin over GM Alireza Firouzja, and he's back this year to defend his title. The star-studded field includes English legends and youngsters alike, as well as multi-generational talents from abroad. On the English side are legendary GMs Michael Adams (55), Luke McShane (42), and Gawain Maroroa Jones (38) to represent the "older guard," with 17-year-old Royal stepping in for Generation Z.

On the international side, American GMs Levon Aronian (44) and Woodward (16) are 27 years and six months apart, and Ukrainian GMs Vasyl Ivanchuk (57) and Samunenkov (17) have 40 years between them. GM Nihal Sarin (22) is from India, and Abdusattorov (also 22) is from Uzbekistan.

This year's event takes place at the London Novotel West in Hammersmith, London, England. But the opening ceremony took place at the iconic Tower of London.

The @xtxmarkets 2026 London Chess Classic opened at the iconic Tower of London! Here are some favourite moments from the opening ceremony. Organised by @schoolschess and sponsored by @xtxmarkets #LondonChessClassic #LCC2026 https://t.co/vu7ZCUz192

— London Chess Classic (@london_chess) November 25, 2026

It's a single round-robin with 10 players and a time control of 90 minutes for 40 moves plus 30 minutes after move 40, with a 30-second increment starting on move one.

Ivanchuk ½-½ Nihal

The first game to end was the encounter of Ivanchuk vs. Nihal, and the Ukrainian grandmaster had some chances to win with an extra pawn. He was "pretty happy" with his opening preparation, he said, and the players followed a GM Magnus Carlsen game from 2006 for the first 19 moves. Nihal played a defensive pawn sacrifice with 21...d5?!, and although Nihal's concept worked, Ivanchuk did have his chances.

In a shrug-your-shoulders tone, Ivanchuk seemed dissatisfied with the draw but gave credit to his opponent. "Okay, hard to be happy because I was clearly better out of the opening, but okay, my opponent defended well," he said.

We saw two more draws in Aronian vs. McShane and Jones vs. Adams. Aronian achieved what might be called a symbolic advantage with White in the Four Knights Spanish; he had a better pawn structure, but no concrete way to make use of that. Adams, on the other hand, had a serious chance to win with Black, but ultimately drew with a pawn for the exchange.

As often happens, the last mistake occurred exactly on move 40, when Adams had just three minutes left before receiving another half hour.

Abdusattorov 1-0 Royal

Abdusattorov's win was praised as the game of the day by the commentators, and indeed it looks like a one-sided bulldozing. The game started as an English Opening, but by move 15 very clearly took on the contours of a Benoni Defense with reversed colors. Abdusattorov's energetic 21.c5? looked great in the game, and it worked out, even if the computer finds some incredible resources for the black pieces. As it happened, the initiative swept Royal off his feet.

Samunenkov 0-1 Woodward

Woodward won his game before Abdusattorov, and this one came from the black side of the Moscow Variation in the Sicilian Defense. Woodward played the combative response 3...Nd7, and by move 12 the position looked like it came out of a Sicilian Najdorf. As is quite typical in the Sicilian Defense—when it goes well for Black—he mounted great pressure down the half-open c-file.

The Challengers group, taking place alongside the Masters, is hardly less exciting and features a world-class field.

GM Mateusz Bartel, GM Rasmus Svane, and IM Carissa Yip lead after the first round.

Standings After Round 1 | Challengers

With the world championship ongoing as well, we will cover this event again after rounds five and nine. Enjoy the show!

The live broadcast was hosted by GMs Daniel King and Stuart Conquest.

The London Chess Classic takes place on November 25-December 4 at the London Novotel West in Hammersmith, London, England. title: Gukesh-Sindarov Game 2 Ends Abruptly In 20-Move London System Draw
summary:
World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju played the London System in game two of the Salesforce FIDE World Championship 2026, but Challenger GM Javokhir Sindarov was ready. Once again, Gukesh fell behind on the clock, but just when Sindarov had gone for a bold pawn push and action seemed to be heating up, the game ended in a 20-move draw by repetition, leaving the scores level at 1-1.

Game three, when Sindarov has the white pieces for a second time, starts Thursday, November 26, at 9 a.m. ET / 15:00 CET / 7:30 p.m. IST.

How to watch the Salesforce FIDE World Championship 2026

You can watch the Salesforce FIDE World Championship 2026 live on Chess.com/Events, Chess.com/TV and on the Chess.com Twitch and YouTube channels, while GM Hikaru Nakamura is streaming on Kick.

The live broadcast is hosted by GMs Judit Polgar and David Howell.

Check out Nakamura's recap of the game, as well as our full playlist with recaps by partner streamers, including IM Levy Rozman.

GM Dejan Bojkov has annotated the game below.

Match Score

Name | | Rating | 01 | 02 | 03 | 04 | 05 | 06 | 07 | 08 | 09 | 10 | 11 | 12 | 13 | 14 | Score

Gukesh Dommaraju | | 2710 | ½ | .½ | . | . | . | . | . | . | . | . | . | . | . | . | 1

Javokhir Sindarov | | 2782 | ½ | ½ | . | . | . | . | . | . | . | . | . | . | . | . | 1

Game two of the match in Geneva was the first time Sindarov would get the black pieces in a world championship game. What was he discussing last-minute with second GM Nikita Vitiugov as they arrived at the venue?

Sindarov arrives for Game 2 and has a discussion with his second Nikita Vitiugov! #GukeshSindarov https://t.co/MASIH5z5kF

— Chess.com News (@ChesscomNews) November 25, 2026

Sindarov later explained: "Not about chess, some mental things. Sometimes not even about chess, some other stuff—just to relax before a game and not be nervous."

Gukesh arrived with his coach, GM Grzegorz Gajewski. Photo: Michal Walusza/FIDE.

Gukesh got to make the first move, choosing 1.d4 (he'd previously played 1.e4 three times and 1.d4 and 1.Nf3 twice each in the world championship match against GM Ding Liren). From there, however, he went on to do something he hadn't done before at this level—play the somewhat infamous London System with 3.Bf4.

The opening used to be associated with unambitious play simply to "get a game," but it's been used extensively by GM Magnus Carlsen and, for instance, by Ding to beat GM Ian Nepomniachtchi in game six of the 2023 World Championship. Gukesh justified his choice as follows:

It’s a good opening! And nowadays everything from both colors is so playable; there’s so much to explore because of engines. I don’t think one opening is better than the others. They’re all possible, and I thought it would be a nice, cool way to start the match!

I thought it would be a nice, cool way to start the match!

—Gukesh Dommaraju on playing the London

As in game one, however, it was Sindarov who played faster in the opening, despite admitting to being somewhat surprised: "Actually I was not expecting the London, but I checked this line before also a lot."

7...Qb6 from Sindarov was the first move that caused Gukesh to think and lose his lead on the clock.

Gukesh didn't think too long, however—six minutes—and when asked at the press conference why he didn't respond 8.Qb3 he explained that the move is hit by 8...Nh5!, before adding that he "knew" 8.Rb1 was the move. The world champion clarified about his opening choices: "I felt I could have remembered more from my notes, but OK, both players are super well-prepared, and getting nothing out of the opening is a very normal outcome in the world championship."

Getting nothing out of the opening is a very normal outcome in the world championship.

—Gukesh Dommaraju

The next move to surprise both commentators and Gukesh was 11...Qd8.

Sindarov's 11...Qd8!? puzzles our commentators. "Gukesh must be confused, just as we are!" (Howell) #GukeshSindarov https://t.co/bMerczwV9h

— Chess.com News (@ChesscomNews) November 25, 2026

Gukesh thought for 25 minutes, while Sindarov, in the press conference, suggested he was proceeding on general principles: "That was the idea of my plan. ...Qd8, and somewhere ...Be8, ...Nd7 [Gukesh admitted he underestimated this plan], ...f5, so I know this idea, and I’m just trying to play somewhere this idea. I think I played it in the best moment!"

When the plan had become obvious to all concerned there was some puzzlement that Sindarov delayed eight minutes before retreating his knight.

After Sindarov takes a long time to play the obvious next move, 14...Nd7, Polgar asks, "How is it possible to spend 8 minutes on this move?" Sindarov yawns — Howell: "Maybe that's why!" #GukeshSindarov https://t.co/xfibR5caXa

— Chess.com News (@ChesscomNews) November 25, 2026

Asked about the yawn afterward, however, Sindarov countered: "I’m good, in general. When my opponent thinks, I’m just trying to chill! I'm not just sleeping there, I'm thinking about the moves."

When my opponent thinks, I'm just trying to chill!

—Javokhir Sindarov

Javokhir Sindarov has so far eased into the world championship match smoothly. Photo: Michal Walusza/FIDE.

When 15...f5! appeared on the board, it was clear the opening had gone well for Sindarov, with Polgar predicting ...g5 to follow in the next five moves with energetic play.

Nothing happened fast, however, with Gukesh spending 30 minutes over the decision to play 16.f3, hinting at e4. When Sindarov brought his knight to f6, however, the e4-break was off the table, as was any real chance of his pushing ...e5.

In the previous world championship match, it didn't worry Gukesh that he had nothing—or was even worse—since he'd invariably try to play on anyway. This time, however, he shut things down by offering a draw by repetition, which Sindarov accepted.

The final moments as Game 2 of the 2026 Salesforce FIDE World Championship ends in a draw by repetition! #GukeshSindarov https://t.co/i053pLi17E

— Chess.com News (@ChesscomNews) November 25, 2026

Gukesh seems to have tempered his willingness to take risks, explaining in the press conference that, "You hope for your opponent to go wrong at some point, but also it's equally likely that you'll get into trouble, so it's about making some clever decisions."

The match is now level at 1-1, with both players looking satisfied with the start. Sindarov explained to FM Mike Klein that although openings are important he still thinks everything will be decided by general chess skills.

Sindarov after Game 2: "Here I'm trying to be better in openings, but in general anyway you'll win a game with good chess—otherwise it's impossible!" #GukeshSindarov https://t.co/3frloTutja

— Chess.com News (@ChesscomNews) November 25, 2026

Gukesh, asked if he'd have preferred to win one of the first two games, quipped, "I’d have preferred both results go my way!" drawing the biggest smile from both players of the post-game interrogation.

Gukesh was in good spirits in the post-game press conference. Photo: Michal Walusza/FIDE.

He added, "I feel energetic on the board," and added, "away from the board I’ve been much happier here compared to Singapore." He put that down to the company of his two friends Charmie Kapoor and Shikhar Saxena.

Gukesh brought two friends with him to Geneva and says he's "become a little more relaxed" than he was when he won the world championship title in Singapore. Photo: Michal Walusza/FIDE.

The battle at the board continues on Thursday, when Sindarov will have White for a second time before the players have their first rest day on Friday. Will we see the Berlin Endgame again?

Mike Klein interviews Sindarov before the players head back to the hotel. Photo: Michal Walusza/FIDE.

title: World-сlass commentary meets cutting-edge technology at the Salesforce FIDE World Championship Match 2026
summary: The Salesforce FIDE World Championship 2026 will be a match to remember. While the players are bringing novelties to the chessboard, the official broadcast on the FIDE YouTube channel is introducing innovations of its own. Viewers can follow every move with world-class commentary, exclusive interviews, AI-powered insights, and live reports directly from the playing venue. The broadcast team brings together some of the most recognizable names in chess. Leading the analysis are grandmasters Peter Svidler and Peter Leko. Svidler is an eight-time Russian Champion and one of the most respected commentators in the chess world, combining elite-level expertise with an engaging style. Leko, a former World Championship challenger, came within half a point of becoming World Champion in his 2004 title match against Vladimir Kramnik. Together, they explain the players’ plans and calculations in a way that is accessible to all chess fans. Grandmaster Maurice Ashley, a fan favourite, serves as host and presenter. He introduces the players before the start of each game, guides viewers through the day’s action, and regularly joins Svidler and Leko in the studio discussion. Meanwhile, charming Charlize van Zyl reports directly from the venue, bringing viewers closer to the championship atmosphere through interviews, behind-the-scenes content, and live updates from the fan zone. Those who missed the opening day should make time to watch the hour-long pre-game show. All four hosts spent an hour discussing the players’ chances, preparation teams, psychological factors, opening expectations, and many of the storylines that could shape the match. Even before the first move was played, it offered valuable insights into what may ultimately decide the world title. It is 2026, and chess broadcasting is evolving with the times. This year’s production introduces several new features that give viewers unique analytical tools and deeper insights into the games. They were developed by none other than Indian Grandmaster Vidit Gujrathi, renowned as a top player, popular streamer, and now, AI developer. Chief Executive Adviser of the FIDE President, Emil Sutovsky explained the vision behind the new setup: “This production represents the first step in an ambitious project – where we aim to transform the fan experience. We gathered a very capable team, which produced a result within short period of time. GM Vidit Gujrathi played a central role in shaping the concept, and together we have laid the foundation for what we see as the future of chess coverage. We will continue developing it over the coming months to deliver the final product in Q2 2027.” Among the most exciting innovations is the FIDE Predictor. Rather than simply calculating the strongest engine move, the Predictor analyses vast numbers of games to estimate which move a human grandmaster is most likely to play in a given position. The prediction is not necessarily the objectively best move. Instead, it attempts to capture human decision-making. As the game unfolds, viewers can compare the prediction with what actually happened on the board, creating a unique opportunity to evaluate both the players and the Predictor itself. GM Vidit Gujrathi shared his perspective on the new tool: “I thought that simply reading out Stockfish moves doesn’t really provide insight into human thinking. So, a while ago, I started developing the Predictor as a fun project. More broadly, I’ve always had the philosophy that we should make chess more exciting and engaging to reach more people. Emil reached out to me, and we quickly realized that we shared the same vision. We started working, but at first we assumed we wouldn’t have enough time to implement it for the World Championship, so we were mainly thinking about future events. But the initial prototype looked good, and we decided to take a chance and use it already in Geneva. It was definitely a risk, but I’m really happy with how the first day went and that a lot of people found it exciting.” The broadcast also provides a wealth of statistical information throughout the game. During Game 1, for example, viewers could immediately see that Gukesh had already spent significantly more time than his opponent in the opening phase, falling 18 minutes behind on the clock after only twelve moves. The “Time Spent” graphic is just one example of the data available. The last five moves are displayed together with their evaluations, allowing viewers to follow the evolution of the position at a glance. According to the engine, the first game featured remarkably accurate play, with no major mistakes from either side. Another feature tracks the players’ winning chances throughout the game. With every move, the agent recalculates the probabilities and updates its assessment. On move 13 of Game 1, the draw probability stood at 62%, with Sindarov given a 21% chance of winning and Gukesh 17%. By move 20, the draw chances had dipped slightly to 59%, while Sindarov’s winning chances increased to 30%.  The commentators were sceptical of such a large gap in Sindarov’s favour from a human perspective, and the agent soon adjusted its assessment. Just one move later, the draw probability returned to 64%, with Sindarov’s chances back at 21% and Gukesh’s at 15%. Such fluctuations provide an additional layer of discussion and entertainment. As fans have come to expect from major FIDE events, the live production combines multiple camera feeds from the playing hall with close-up shots of the players and the board, alongside a digital board displaying the position with complete clarity.  The commentators demonstrate possible variations, helping viewers understand not only what happened in the game but also the ideas and calculations that remained behind the scenes. The broadcast also features distinguished guests. On the opening day, Viswanathan Anand, former World Champion and one of the greatest players in chess history, joined the studio. As always, Anand brought valuable insights drawn from his own World Championship experience, adding another dimension to the analysis. Whether you are a dedicated chess fan or following the World Championship for the first time, the FIDE Channel offers far more than a simple live board. With elite commentary,

title: Salesforce FIDE World Championship Match: Gukesh and Sindarov size each other up
summary: Game two of the Salesforce FIDE World Championship Match 2026 in Geneva ended in a draw after just 2 hours and 20 moves. Both contenders eventually concluded that there was little the position could offer to upset the balance. Today, the ceremonial first move was played by H.E. Erzhan KAZYKHAN, Permanent Representative of the Republic of Kazakhstan to the United Nations Office and other International Organizations in Geneva. It was thanks to this senior diplomat that the press conference ahead of the opening ceremony could take place in Room XIV at the Palais des Nations. Unlike yesterday, the guest’s choice did not match the move Gukesh had intended to play. The Indian put his e-pawn back on its starting square and opted for 1.d4 instead. The game opened with the London System, a solid setup that generally allows both sides to develop their pieces naturally. Gukesh has plenty of experience with this opening from the white side. His most recent success with it dates back to the India–Uzbekistan match at the Olympiad in Samarkand last September, when he defeated Sindarov’s teammate Ortik Nigmatov. Although Black has several reasonable ways to meet the London System, Sindarov followed the aforementioned game until the sixth move. Both players seemed familiar with the line up to around move 10, when they began spending more time on their decisions. Gukesh gradually arranged his pieces in preparation for the first clash between the two armies. Sindarov, meanwhile, manoeuvred efficiently, using little time while maintaining a solid position. After 15…f5, Gukesh took some time to assess whether the position could be opened up. He may have been tempted to try 17.c4, either on this move or the previous one, but evidently did not consider his position promising enough to enter the ensuing complications. One possible continuation is 17…cxd4 18.exd4 dxc4 19.Bxc4 Nd5! 20.Qxe6+ Bf7 21.Qe2 Bg5, when Black enjoys very active piece play as compensation for the sacrificed pawn. Sindarov admitted afterwards that he had not calculated the consequences of the c4-break precisely, as he felt the position was not yet ripe for such a break. Gukesh astutely added that a draw seemed the natural outcome at that point, since he could not see how either side could achieve anything through a pawn break. There is an old proverb that says, “Pawns are the soul of chess.” Clearly, in this game, with no promising pawn break on the horizon, both contenders became dispirited and eventually settled for a draw. In retrospect, Gukesh was not disappointed with either the nature or the outcome of the game. At the post-round press conference, he explained that it often happens that Black manages to neutralise White’s opening idea, leaving little room for further progress. So early in the match, he felt there was no reason to take unnecessary risks. Javokhir Sindarov will have the white pieces for the second time in the match tomorrow, when game three is scheduled to take place at 3 p.m. on Thursday, November 26, at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, Geneva. FACT SHEET – Game 2, Salesforce FIDE World Championship Match 2026 White: Gukesh Dommaraju Black: Javokhir Sindarov Result: ½–½ Opening: London System Game length: 20 moves Match score: 1–1 Meanwhile, in the fan zone, GM Anna Muzychuk challenged chess enthusiasts to a series of “Hand & Brain” games. The concept involves two pairs of players facing each other in a single game. Within each team, the player assigned the role of “Brain” announces the name of the piece that should move, while their partner, the “Hand”, decides which move to play. The inevitable misunderstandings between teammates are part of what makes the format so entertaining! And in the end, even the champion and her partner were beaten by a pair of strong amateurs. Written by Yannick Pelletier Photos: Michal Walusza The Salesforce FIDE World Championship Match 2026 is taking place at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, near Geneva, Switzerland, from November 22 to December 12. All information on the schedule can be found on the Championship website. Tickets to the playing hall and the fan zone can be purchased on the designated website: https://tickets.fide.com/en , while games can be watched on the FIDE YouTube channel with live commentaries by top Grandmasters Peter Leko and Peter Svidler.

title: World Championship Game 2: A London in Geneva
summary:
Gukesh Dommaraju and Javokhir Sindarov drew the second game of their World Championship match in Geneva on Wednesday. Playing white for the first time, Gukesh opted for the London System, but found his opponent well-prepared to deal with the relatively cautious opening choice. The defending champion spent considerable time on two key decisions before opting for a threefold repetition. The contenders appear to be testing each other's preparation at this early stage. | Photo: FIDE / Michal Walusza

A 20-move draw

Gukesh Dommaraju had the white pieces for the first time in his World Championship match against Javokhir Sindarov on Wednesday. Given his reputation as a player who is almost always looking to play for a win - sometimes even to a fault - few would have been surprised had Gukesh opted for an ambitious opening system. Instead, the defending champion went for the London System: 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bf4 .

Curiously, the London System made an appearance in Geneva on the very day that the strong London Chess Classic , featuring the likes of Nodirbek Abdusattorov and Vasyl Ivanchuk, got under way in the English capital.

While the system is often regarded as a rather cautious, positional approach, Gukesh spoke favourably of the opening at the post-game press conference:

I don't know why it gets so much hate, it's a cool opening.

Reigning champion Gukesh Dommaraju was in a good mood in the post-game press conference | Photo: Michal Walusza

Commentator Peter Svidler suggested that Gukesh's choice might serve a longer-term strategic purpose. By employing the London, the defending champion could test Sindarov's opening preparation without revealing the lines he has prepared for when he feels the time is right to make a more ambitious attempt at a win.

Despite its popularity at club level and its increasing presence in elite chess, the London System has rarely featured in World Championship matches. In fact, Ding Liren is the only player to have won a game with the system in a match for the world title, having obtained a crucial victory over Ian Nepomniachtchi in game six of their 2023 encounter in Astana. Ding would later employ the London twice against Gukesh at their 2024 match in Singapore, drawing both games six and ten.

A London System on the board during game two of the match at the Fondation Martin Bodmer | Photo: Michal Walusza

Much as in Tuesday's opening encounter, Sindarov was the quicker of the two players in the opening phase, although Gukesh was clearly still within the bounds of his preparation.

The first real surprise came when Sindarov retreated his queen with 11...Qd8 . Peter Leko, himself a remarkable positional player, was impressed by the challenger's approach and the quality of his preparation. Gukesh, meanwhile, spent around 25 minutes before replying with 12.0-0

A few moves later, following Sindarov's 15...f5 , Gukesh again went into a lengthy think. By this point, it was clear that the Uzbek grandmaster knew exactly how to handle the setup, having comfortably achieved equality. The defending champion spent nearly half an hour before opting for 16.f3 , preparing the central pawn push e3-e4.

After Sindarov's 16...Nf6 , which discouraged the intended pawn advance, Gukesh signalled his willingness to settle for a draw with 17.Be5 . Following 17...Nd7 18.Bg3 , the players repeated the position three times, bringing the second game of the match to an end.

Unlike Tuesday's opener in the Berlin Defence , Wednesday's encounter offered little in the way of tension. At this early stage of the match, the two contenders appear to be probing each other's opening preparation.

Judging by his clock management in the first two games, Sindarov seems to be either better prepared or more confident than his opponent. Gukesh, on the other hand, appears content to ease his way into the match. After all, a 14-game World Championship match is more of a marathon than a sprint.
